en: In the *Rāṣṭrapālasūtra*, it is said: "The Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kuru country, arrived at Sthūlakoṣṭhaka. He stayed at Sthūlakoṣṭhaka in the grove of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka.
The brahmins and householders of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kuru country..."

They arrived at Sthūlakoṣṭhaka; he arrived at Sthūlakoṣṭhaka; he dwelt at Sthūlakoṣṭhaka in the grove of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka. And having heard this, they gathered from group to group and from community to community, assembling and coming together.
Emerging from Sthūlakoṣṭhaka, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As the Brahmins and householders of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dharma.

At that time, Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, was seated and present in that assembly. Then, this thought occurred to Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder: "As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has spoken, it is not easy for one living in the midst of a household to maintain, for as long as life lasts, a state that is entirely white, pure, complete, and perfect."

"I wish to lead the holy life, completely pure and cleansed. Suppose I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and out of right faith go forth from the home to the homeless state. Then the Blessed One, in many ways, instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the brahmins and householders of Sthūlakoṣṭhika with a discourse on the Dharma.
He became silent.

Then the brahmins and householders of Sthūlakoṣṭhika, having rejoiced and approved of what the Blessed One had spoken, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from his presence. The householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla remained right there.

Then, the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla, perceiving that the brahmins and householders of Sthūlakoṣṭhika had not long since departed, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One,
addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
“I would lead the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One, [attaining] the state of a monk.
“Have you been permitted by your parents, son of a householder? “No, Venerable Sir.”
"For indeed, householder’s son, neither a Tathāgata nor a disciple of a Tathāgata ordains or grants full admission to one who has not been permitted by his parents.
"Venerable Sir, I shall act in such a way that my parents will grant permission.
Then Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the presence of the Blessed One.
Then Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, went to his own residence and addressed his mother and father:

"Mother, Father, give me your permission; I shall go forth from home into homelessness with perfect faith. "Dear Rāṣṭrapāla, you should know this: you are our only son, beloved, pleasing, patient, and never disagreeable. Even at the cost of death, we would remain separated from you against our will; how much more so [while you are alive]?"
"Furthermore, we shall release him while he is still alive.

If you grant permission, that would be well; if you do not grant permission, from this day forward I shall not even eat food. Then Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, underwent one meal-skip; he underwent two, three, and so on, up to seven meal-skips.
Then the parents of the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla said this to the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla:
"My dear Rāṣṭrapāla, you should know that you are indeed delicate and accustomed to comfort; you do not know suffering.
The holy life is difficult to practice, solitude is difficult to endure, dwelling alone is difficult to find joy in, and the higher realizations are difficult to awaken to."
"Go to dwell in remote lodgings in forest retreats and wilderness tracts. But you, my dear Rāṣṭrapāla, remain right here;
enjoy sensual pleasures, give gifts, and perform meritorious deeds.
When he had been addressed thus, Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, remained silent.

Then Rāṣṭrapāla’s parents incited his kinsmen: "Come now, kinsmen, raise up our dear Rāṣṭrapāla. Then the kinsmen approached where Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, was; having approached, they said this to Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son:
"Dear Rāṣṭrapāla, you should know that you are indeed delicate and accustomed to comfort; you do not understand suffering, as before [stated]. Therefore, perform meritorious deeds."

Thus addressed, Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, remained silent. Then Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, urged his parents and his friends, saying: "Come now, friends, please raise up my father, Rāṣṭrapāla.
Then Rāṣṭrapāla’s friends approached where Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, was; having approached, they said this to Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son.

"Indeed, gentle Rāṣṭrapāla, you should know this: you are delicate and a seeker of pleasure; you do not understand suffering as previously described, so perform meritorious deeds. When he had been addressed thus, Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, remained silent.
Then the companions of Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, approached the parents of Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son. Having approached...
He said this to his mother and father:
"Mother and father, please grant permission for your son Rāṣṭrapāla to go forth into the religious life. What will you do with him dead?
If he finds delight [in the teaching], you shall see him alive; if he does not find delight, what other destination is there for a son?"
"Except for our mother and father.
Thus, young man, we give our permission to you, Rāṣṭrapāla, provided that after you have gone forth, you will show yourself [to us].
Then the friends of Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, approached where Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, was; having approached, they said this to Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder:

"Indeed, gentle Rāṣṭrapāla, you should know this: if you have been permitted by your parents, then having gone forth, you must present yourself [before me]. Then, Rāṣṭrapāla, the householder’s son, gradually regaining the physical vigor and strength of his body, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. To one side...
Standing there, Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable Sir, I have been permitted by my mother and father; may I receive the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya? May I practice the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having obtained permission, Rāṣṭrapāla, the son of a householder, received the going-forth, the full ordination, and the status of a monk in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.

Then the Blessed One, having caused the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla to go forth and having conferred full ordination upon him, dwelt at Sthūlakoṣṭhaka for as long as he pleased and then set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī. Traveling by stages, he arrived at Śrāvastī and stayed there in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.

Now at that time, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s father was shaving a shaven-headed man in the middle gate-hall. The venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s father saw the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla near the gate. Having seen him, he said this: "Those shaven-headed ascetics have brought ruin upon our family!"
"By whom was our only son, Rāṣṭrapāla—who is dear, beloved, patient, and not disagreeable—to us made to go forth and ordained?
Who thinks that alms should be given to or service should be performed for those shaven-headed śramaṇas?
Thus, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla received no gift other than abuse in his own home; he departed from there very quickly.

Now at that time, the venerable Rāṣḍrapāla’s old, worn-out slave-girl had scattered some stale, putrid boiled grain and gone outside to discard it. Then that old servant woman went very quickly to where the elder of the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla was; having approached him, she said this to the elder of the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla: "Master, you should know that the gentle Rāṣṭrapāla has arrived at Sthūlakoṣṭaka long ago, yet he does not wish to enter his own residence."
Then the elder of the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, gathering his hair with his left hand and putting on a single-layered robe, approached the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla.
At that time, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla was standing on the edge of the rampart, eating some stale, putrid gruel.

Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s mother-in-law: "Even by doing this, I am unable to turn my son-in-law Rāṣṭrapāla back. What if I were to urge the daughters-in-law? Then the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s mother-in-law, urging the daughters-in-law, said this: Mat_40: "Daughters-in-law, go to your husband Rāṣṭrapāla and say to him: 'Sir, why do you not take pleasure in the pleasures of the five senses as you did before? Sir, we have heard that those who do not take pleasure in the pleasures of the five senses as they did before will, after death, at the breaking up of the body, be reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the abyss, hell. Mat_41: Then the daughters-in-law went to the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla and said to him: "Sir, why do you not take pleasure in the pleasures of the five senses as you did before? Sir, we have heard that those who do not take pleasure in the pleasures of the five senses as they did before will, after death, at the breaking up of the body, be reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the abyss, hell. Mat_42: When this was said, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla said to the daughters-in-law: "Daughters-in-law, I do not take pleasure in the pleasures of the five senses as I did before, nor do I delight in them. Daughters-in-law, I take pleasure in other things than the pleasures of the five senses; I delight in them. Mat_43: When this was said, the daughters-in-law said to the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla: "Sir, what are those other things in which you take pleasure, and in which you delight, instead of the pleasures of the five senses? Mat_44: When this was said, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla said to the daughters-in-law: "Daughters-in-law, it is like a man who has a house with many stories, with a single entrance, well-secured and protected, where there are many rats. Those rats, coming out through the entrance, would gnaw at the rafters, the beams, the pillars, and the walls. Then a man would come from somewhere, one who knows houses and understands the nature of houses. Having looked at that house, he would think: 'This house has many stories, with a single entrance, well-secured and protected, yet there are many rats. These rats, coming out through the entrance, gnaw at the rafters, the beams, the pillars, and the walls. Having seen this, he would think: 'I must quickly build another house with many stories, with a single entrance, well-secured and protected, where there are no rats. Having built that house, he would think: 'Those rats, coming out through the entrance, gnawed at the rafters, the beams, the pillars, and the walls of my former house; now they gnaw at the rafters, the beams, the pillars, and the walls of this house. Daughters-in-law, I am like that man. My body is like that house. The eye is its entrance, the ear its entrance, the nose its entrance, the tongue its entrance, the body its entrance, and the mind its entrance. Through the eye, forms enter; through the ear, sounds enter; through the nose, odors enter; through the tongue, tastes enter; through the body, tangibles enter; and through the mind, mental objects enter. Those mental objects, having entered through the mind, gnaw at the rafters, the beams, the pillars, and the walls of my body. Daughters-in-law, I am like that man who, seeing this, thinks: 'I must quickly build another house with many stories, with a single entrance, well-secured and protected, where there are no rats. Daughters-in-law, I am like that man who has built that house. Those rats, coming out through the entrance, gnaw at the rafters, the beams, the pillars, and the walls of my former house; now they gnaw at the rafters, the beams, the pillars, and the walls of this house. Daughters-in-law, I am like that man who, seeing this, thinks: 'Those rats gnawed at the rafters, the beams, the pillars, and the walls of my former house; now they gnaw at the rafters, the beams, the pillars, and the walls of this house. O bride, with the same forms by which you were formerly bathed, clothed in garments, adorned with ornaments, perfumed with incense,
and sprinkled with powders when you were the beloved and charming wife of Rāṣṭrapāla while he was still a householder—
bathed with those very baths, clothed in those garments, adorned with those ornaments, and perfumed with those incenses...
Covered with powders, one fell at one foot and the second at the other, and spoke thus:
"Of what appearance are those celestial nymphs for whose sake the noble son practices the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One?
Then, as before, the former wife of the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, having bathed with such baths and [anointed] with powders...
They were dusted with powder by Rāṣṭrapāla. When he was formerly a householder, they had been dear and pleasing to him;

they bathed with such baths as those previously described, and so on until they were dusted with powder. One fell at one foot and the second at the other. Such were those celestial nymphs for whose sake the noble son practices the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One. (Mat_42)
"Sisters, it is not for the sake of the apsarases that I lead the holy life in the presence of the Blessed One.
(Mat 43) Then, when the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla was addressed with the title "sister" by his former second wife, she fainted and fell to the ground.

(Mat 44) Then the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla addressed his parents: "Mother and father, if food has been renounced, why is it not sold? Why is that which has been renounced treated with such distress? (Mat 45)
"Eat, dear Rāṣṭrapāla!

Then the elderly man and the elderly woman of the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s family personally satisfied and served the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla with various kinds of pure and excellent foods, both hard and soft. In many ways, with pure...
Having personally satisfied and served him with excellent solid and soft foods,

and having perceived that the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla had finished eating, washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, she took a lower seat and sat down to hear the Dharma. Then, at that time, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla spoke these verses:

"O King, for one who possesses the wisdom of grasping, the life of a recluse alone is better. Then, Great King Kauravya, having rejoiced and approved of what the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla had spoken, bowed his head at the feet of the venerable one, rose from his seat, and departed.
